extracted.intended_audience: college/university mathematics instructors (those designing assessment for undergraduate math courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for designing and running group-based, cooperative, and problem-centered assessment activities (reviews, quizzes, collaborative exams, oral take-home exams, and cooperative-learning structures) in undergraduate mathematics courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group Exam Review (worksheet/board consensus method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand out a worksheet of problems to review; divide class into groups; each group solves one problem and posts the solution on the board; groups continue solving and posting; instructor marks a problem 'solved' when several groups agree and leads whole-class work when there is disagreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: Students like the approach, spend class actively solving problems, form study contacts, and end with a completed solution set. Use: motivates students to study and helps them identify what they do and don't know; useful as exam preparation. Note the method covers many problems in limited time and leaves individuals having actively wrestled with only some problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think–Pair–Share
rubrics_metrics.description: Pose a problem, give students time to think individually, then pair them to share and agree on a solution, then have pairs report to the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: Prevents most-prepared students from dominating, forces individual thinking, increases confidence before whole-class sharing. Use: most useful when introducing a new concept; use sparingly because of class time cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quiz for Two / Quiz Consulting
rubrics_metrics.description: Quiz for Two: students take a quiz in pairs; Quiz Consulting: students may leave their desks to briefly discuss the quiz (or talk for one minute during a quiz) but must leave written work at their desks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: Students learn during assessment, performance rises, anxiety declines. Use: allows instructor to set somewhat more challenging problems but beware overdoing it (may raise anxiety). Verbal discussion-only forces articulation of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative Exams — Option 1 (class discussion during timed multiple choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give an extremely challenging multiple-choice exam and allow class discussion during the exam while each student ultimately turns in their own solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example used in large classes. Risk: students may defer to a 'smartest' peer to maximize grade rather than learn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative Exams — Option 2 (individual then group answer sheets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a shorter exam to be taken twice: first individually (turn in answers), then allow small-group discussion and submit a group answer sheet at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: students can discuss more deeply after personal thinking; discussion can deteriorate into grade-guessing. Use: final score can be the average of the two scores to combine individual accountability and group learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design assessments to promote learning not just measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use group-based assessment methods that reduce anxiety, foster team spirit, and make quizzes/exams part of the learning process rather than mere regurgitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings across methods: group activities lead to deeper learning, reduced exam anxiety, and perception of quizzes as learning exercises. Vary assessment methods to minimize weaknesses of any single approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate assessment plan and grading early
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss the assessment plan and cooperative-learning expectations at the start of the course; include dates and relative weights in the syllabus; use a midterm report to illustrate grade computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: motivates participation and avoids misunderstandings; clarifying that individual work may count more heavily later helps manage student expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group composition and management guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with group sizes and composition; common practices include groups of 3–4 (more successful than 4–5), heterogeneous or purposefully arranged groups, frequent rearrangement, and optional role assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tips: rearrange groups frequently, sometimes group by similarity or mix dominant and quiet students, have students fill info cards to help pairing, allow leadership to emerge naturally or assign roles (record keeper, questioner, leader). If some students refuse group work, group them together so others' experience isn't spoiled; provide specific objectives and timelines to keep groups on task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide group-work norms/guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Give students explicit behavioral guidelines for group work (e.g., listen openly, support objective/logical solutions, avoid conflict-reducing tricks like majority vote or coin toss).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference existing cooperative-learning guidelines (e.g., Johnson & Johnson). Use these to encourage constructive collaboration and discourage superficial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use weekly journals and instructor feedback to detect and address misconceptions early
rubrics_metrics.description: Read group and individual work (journals) regularly to track progress and immediately address widespread weaknesses via class discussion or targeted activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when groups repeatedly misapplied a theorem, the instructor discussed the error in class and gave a related exercise to prevent recurrence. Journals also allow private instructor responses or group conferences about personal issues affecting participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneous grouping for cooperative activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Form groups heterogeneously (mixing sex, ability, age, personality) of four students (or five when necessary) for most cooperative activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings: heterogeneous groups facilitate varied interactions; for Teams-Games-Tournaments, temporarily form homogeneous ability groups for competition, then return points to original heterogeneous teams. Adjust group size as appropriate for activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teams–Games–Tournaments (TGT) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: TGT consists of teaching, team study, and tournament games: groups split into homogeneous ability subgroups to answer numbered questions, winners keep cards, points are converted to team averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use at chapter conclusions for review. Allow challenges of answers; sometimes follow-up with a graded individual quiz based on randomly selected tournament questions. Findings: gives weaker students chances to shine; avoid counting team averages toward grades if students perceive unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jigsaw expert-group method
rubrics_metrics.description: Each team member becomes an expert on a subtopic, joins with other 'experts' to master it, then returns to teach their original team; teacher acts as facilitator posing guiding questions rather than lecturing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome: students become responsible for teaching all team members; teacher monitors for accuracy and provides probing questions to lead students to correct conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment-Along as peer-assessment of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Students write questions and answers as homework; teams evaluate and edit answers in sequence across multiple teams and finally present consolidated conclusions to the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This activity provides assessment of students' own reasoning and immediate feedback on the validity of judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative Oral Take-Home Exam (COTHE) instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: COTHE is open-note/open-book/open-group; distribute the exam a week in advance; groups (no larger than 3 unless permitted) work together, cite resources, sign up for a 30-minute oral appointment, submit written work, and are graded on oral demonstration of understanding rather than on the written work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral procedure: interviewer selects one student at a time to answer while others remain silent; after the answer the group may add/amend and no answer is accepted until the entire group agrees. Schedule spill-over time between appointments. Benefits: deep insight into student thinking, immediate formative feedback, encourages discussion of study habits. Do not permit discussing with people outside the group (except instructor) — such discussions constitute plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: COTHE grading protocol and face-to-face feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign grades during the oral appointment and explain strengths/weaknesses face-to-face; emphasize larger learning expectations rather than point deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving grades, explain specific reasons and areas for improvement; frame comments as high expectations and temporary shortcomings rather than personal failure. Face-to-face grading encourages follow-up conversations about study habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid point-based micro-grading for COTHEs
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assign grades by many small point deductions; point-based schemes can misrepresent students' conceptual knowledge and lead to awkward grade bands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grades tend to bunch up with COTHEs; instead use broader criteria-based judgments to differentiate performance more meaningfully (see next metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and share larger grading criteria beforehand (COTHE and similar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish and share broad grading categories with students such as mechanics, concepts, and problem solving prior to the exam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics: algebra skills and tool use (e.g., graphing calculator); Concepts: understanding principles and linking concepts; Problem solving: reading mathematics, trying multiple approaches. Provide at least cursory feedback on each area when grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design exam problems to be forward- and backward-looking
rubrics_metrics.description: Create problems that both assess past learning and prepare students for upcoming material; include tasks that require reading a text and learning new mathematics so interviews can both assess and teach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the oral interviews to build on students' current understandings and address trouble spots revealed during the exam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a two-part approach when individual accountability is a concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine a collaborative assessment (e.g., COTHE) with an individual follow-up (in-class questions) to ensure individual accountability and diagnosis of weak students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a two-part exam (collaborative oral followed by individual in-class questions) or the 'pyramid' exam model; useful when instructor is worried about missing individual weaknesses early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-centered course assessment principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment should occur while students are engaged in problem solving (integrated with learning) rather than as a separate activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To promote reflection and authentic problem-solving, emphasize students' explanations and methods over prescribed procedures; negotiate classroom norms focusing on reasoning and reconstruction of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback-focused grading (comments over points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide written feedback comments on students' problem solutions rather than assigning points; use these comments to guide students' progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall course grading still includes classwork, homework, midterm, and final, but grades should reflect progress toward competence in mathematical problem solving rather than a simple weighted average of numeric scores. Discuss assessment plan and goals with students at course start and revisit as needed.
